drills.coachNote: With you completely winning, White's only practical hope is to keep queens on and stir up threats with Qh5 near your king — his rook on d1 is otherwise just hanging. Qxa3 grabs a pawn but leaves that queen active; after Qxf5 it digs into your kingside, and Qxb4 Rc1 Qf4 turns into a real fight, costing 2.1 pawns of your edge. Qxd1! forces the issue instead — after Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 you trade queen and bishop for rook and queen, banking the exchange with queens off entirely. drills.coachNote: White's knight on f3 wants to hop into g5, forking ideas against your bishop on e6 and creeping toward h7 near your own king — that's the move you need to answer. Bf6 retreats passively and ignores it completely; after Ng5 Bxg5 Qxg5 f4, pieces get traded off and White's queen recentralizes, handing back 1.6 pawns of your winning position. Bxf2+! was sitting there instead — it wins a pawn with check, and after Kh1 Bf7 Qg5 Bxe1 Rxe1 your bishop mops up the exchange too, since the forced king move leaves the rook on e1 undefended. When the enemy king only has pawns for cover, always look for the check before playing a quiet retreat.

drills.coachNote: Black's knight on b4 is staring at your bishop on d3, and nothing defends it — play anything else and it's simply gone. Rc7! fights back by force instead, invading the seventh rank to hit your queen on d7; after Qxc7 Nxc7 Bxd3 Re1 Kxc7 you've traded queen for rook and knight, a far smaller deficit than losing the bishop for nothing. Kf3 is the tidier route — it backs up e4 and heads toward the center efficiently, and after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 Kf7 your pawns march home without Black's king ever getting a foothold.
